say: Tick each item. You need your NIN and BVN, an account in your own name with your own PIN, and alerts coming to your own phone.

Keep a register of every asset, whose name is on it and your share. For example, Amaka in Onitsha found she had contributed 800,000 naira of 2,000,000 for a plot, which is 40%. She photographed every receipt and kept copies safe.
And name a next of kin on every account, so money can reach your children without delay.

panel.heading: Financial independence checklist
items: NIN and BVN in place
An account in my own name
My own phone for alerts
Asset register with copies
Next of kin named everywhere

say: No bank, regulator or genuine agent will ask for your PIN or OTP. If you think someone knows it, change it immediately in your app or at a branch.

panel.heading: Keep yourself and your money safe

cards.d: No bank or genuine agent asks for your PIN, password or OTP. Do not let anyone use your accounts with it.
Taking all your earnings or forcing loans in your name is financial abuse. Safety comes first.
People pose as bank staff online and charge to fix complaints. Use only official contacts.

say: If a partner takes all your earnings, refuses you any money or forces loans in your name, that is financial abuse, not a normal disagreement. Keep some money and copies of documents where only you can reach them, and talk to someone you trust.

say: And beware people who pose as bank staff on social media. Use only contact details from the official website or app.

say: At a bank, a fintech or a cooperative, these six questions put you in control. First, what is the total I will earn or pay, in naira?

say: For example, Grace has 300,000 naira she will not need for six months. A fixed deposit at 12% a year earns 18,000 naira in six months, but has a penalty for early withdrawal.

A flexible wallet at 8% earns 12,000 naira, and she can withdraw any time. She checks the wallet is licensed by the CBN, keeps one month of emergency money in it, and puts the rest in the fixed deposit. She chose by naira and access, not by the advert.

Read your statement every month for charges or transfers you do not recognise. If something is wrong, complain to the provider in writing with dates, amounts and screenshots, and ask for a reference number.

panel.heading: Complain in writing, then escalate
items: First: the provider, in writing, get a reference
Banks and wallets: the CBN
Digital lenders: the FCCPC
Insurers: NAICOM
Pension administrators: PenCom
Investment firms: the SEC

say: If it is not solved, escalate to the right regulator. The CBN for banks and wallets, the FCCPC for digital lenders, NAICOM for insurers, PenCom for pensions and the SEC for investment firms.

say: Your capstone is a Personal Financial Management Plan, and its heart is one SMART goal: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Funke's health check showed only two weeks of emergency cover.
She wants one month of essential costs, 180,000 naira. She already has 90,000.

card.title: Funke's SMART goal
rows: Goal: one month of essential costs

say: So she needs 90,000 naira more.

card.title: Funke's SMART goal
rows: Goal: one month of essential costs

say: Her surplus is about 40,000 naira a month, so she saves 30,000 and keeps 10,000 as a margin for slow weeks. That is about 7,000 naira every Monday.
Her milestones: 120,000 by day 30, 150,000 by day 60, and 180,000 by day 90. If a hard month comes, she lowers the amount instead of abandoning the plan.

card.title: Funke's SMART goal

say: To remember. Keep an account and records in your own name. Never share your PIN. Ask the six questions. Complain in writing first.
And turn your goal into weekly actions, then review weekly, monthly and quarterly.

panel.heading: Remember

Complain in writing, then to the regulator
SMART goal, weekly action, 30-day milestones

say: Now start your asset and document register. Ask two providers the six questions and compare them in naira. Then write your SMART goal and three dated milestones.
